#69465. Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reiver

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software.
  • It has been revealed that every numbered statement below is false.
  • It has been revealed that these are not made up for effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software. That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles. This article ("Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto") is my one of my contributions to that genre.

It has been revealed that every numbered statement below is false. Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

It has been revealed that these are not made up for effect. Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

Industry observers note that handles can change. The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it (DIDs) “unique and immutable”.

My handle changed! My handle was first reiver.bsky.social, then became reiver.myatproto.social, and then later became reiver.blacksky.team. You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit. (did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID.).

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Use the DID. Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID's handle is from time to time.

But, you need to normalize the DID before using it. As, for example, did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz as the same DID.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team.

It has been revealed that A latest handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one. joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine. Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

For example, Bluesky's own account (did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social, and then became bsky.app. You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit. (Another reason to key consumers by DID, and not by any part of their handle.).

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

A handle can change at any moment. The user can switch to a upcoming handle. The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else. Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving. The handle specification notes “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”.

So, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it. The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”. Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes. And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID.

An account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it. The DID specification claims “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”.

Sources indicate that in API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).” And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional. So, your code needs a “no handle” case.

Every handle ends in .bsky.social.

Recent findings suggest that any Internet domain can be a handle. And, other PDSes hand out their own — the blacksky.app PDS, for example, offers .blacksky.app, .myatproto.social, .cryptoanarchy.network, and others.

Even if a user's handle is not a .bsky.social handle now, their first handle was.

A user's first handle is whatever they got when their account was created — on whichever PDS they signed up with. com.atproto.server.createAccount just takes a “Requested handle for the account”, and each PDS offers its own domains. So, someone who signed up on blacksky.app might start out as alice.myatproto.social — and never have had a .bsky.social handle at all.

In a recent development, you can see this in a DID's audit log on plc.directory (https://plc.directory//log/audit) — the very first operation (the one that created the DID) shows the first handle, and the first PDS. For example, the audit log for did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w (plc.directory/did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w/log/audit) has just 1 operation — the one that created it, on November 13th, 2026. Its first handle was shadowoftruth.myatproto.social, and its first PDS was blacksky.app. It has never had a .bsky.social handle.

A handle is a third-level domain — like alice.bsky.social, alice.blacksky.app, or alice.myatproto.social.

It has been revealed that A handle can have any number of segments, as long as there are at least 2. example.com is a valid handle — and so is apple.banana.cherry.example.com. The handle specification only indicates “there must be at least two segments” (so a bare top-level domain like com is not allowed), each segment can be 1 to 63 characters, and the whole handle can be at most 253 characters. Its own examples include a.co, 8.cn, and XX.LCS.MIT.EDU; and the official test vectors include john.test.bsky.app, and a valid handle with 10 segments.

Sources indicate that with DNS (a TXT record at _atproto.) or HTTPS (/.well-known/atproto-did). You need to support both.

If a DID document lists a handle, the account owns that handle.

In a recent development, anyone can put any handle in their own DID document. The handle has to resolve back to the same DID — both directions must agree. Otherwise, show handle.invalid.

com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle checks both directions for you.

Its own lexicon claims it “Does not necessarily bi-directionally verify against the the DID document.” (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

did:web is supported too. Your code needs to handle both.

In ATProto, “did:web is restricted in atproto to only full domains, not paths or port specification” (from the record key specification).

Whatever plc.directory returns for a DID is that DID's document.

In a recent development, check that the document's id matches the DID you asked for. (See: How-To Resolve a DID to a PDS.).

A did:plc is case-insensitive — so DID:PLC:… or did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR is fine.

Recent findings suggest that the did: and the method name (plc) must be lowercase — “The URI starts with lowercase did:”, and “The method segment is one or more lowercase letters”. And, a did:plc identifier is lowercase too: “the entire identifier is lower-case (and should be normalized to lower-case)” (from the did:plc specification). The ATProto specification says “protocol implementations should reject DIDs with invalid casing.” (plc.directory answered did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR, did:PLC:…, and DID:PLC:… with 400 “Resolution of non-PLC DIDs not supported”.).

DIDs are case-sensitive — so did:plc:abc… and did:plc:ABC… are 2 different accounts.

For did:plc, the uppercase one is not a different DID — it is not a valid did:plc at all, since its identifier is lowercase-only base32. The ATProto specification states “the presently-supported methods are not case sensitive, and could be safely lowercased”, and that “It is permissible to attempt case normalization when receiving user-controlled input, such as when parsing public URL path components, or text input fields.” So: reject bad casing in protocol data; lowercasing what a user typed is fine.

If a DID parser accepts it, it is a valid DID.

Recent findings suggest that A generic DID parser only checks the generic syntax — which allows uppercase in the identifier (the test vectors list did:method:VAL as valid). The indigo library's syntax.ParseDID accepts did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR — but plc.directory rejects it. Generic syntax is not the same as a valid did:plc.

A did:plc's DID document never changes.

Sources indicate that the DID never changes — but its DID document can. Each change is a signed operation, and the handle (alsoKnownAs), the PDS (the #atproto_pds service), the signing key (#atproto), and the rotation keys can all be changed.

For example, my DID's audit log (plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit) has 4 operations:.

And, the did:plc specification has 2 more surprises. A “tombstone” operation “clears all of the data fields and permanently deactivates the DID”. And, there is a 72-hour window during which a higher-authority rotation key can “"rewrite" history”. So, do not cache a DID document forever — re-resolve it from time to time, and watch the firehose for #identity events.

“Personal” Data Server means one server per person.

“Many PDSes will host multiple people” (the glossary). Most host many.

Bluesky consumers' data is on bsky.social.

The server a user logs in at is the server that has their data.

In a recent development, it might be an entryway — a separate OAuth server for many PDSes. puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network's /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource lists https://bsky.social as its authorization server. (blacksky.app, on the other hand, lists itself.).

According to recent reports, accounts can migrate to another PDS — that is a core design goal. Always look up the current PDS from the DID document (and do not cache it forever).

A user's PDS can show them everyone's posts.

In a recent development, A PDS only has its own accounts' data. For timelines, threads, and counts, it forwards the request to an AppView. (See: ATProto PDS.).

A user's PDS builds (or renders) their timeline.

According to recent reports, the timeline (app.bsky.feed.getTimeline) is built by an AppView. The PDS just forwards the app's request to it. And, no server renders it — the AppView returns JSON, and the app (on the user's phone or computer) renders that.

(This one used to be closer to true. Bluesky's feed generator starter kit still says “In the future, the PDS will hydrate the feed with the help of an App View, but for now, the PDS handles hydration itself.” Today, the AppView does it. See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

Bluesky's PDS software is the only PDS software.

Sources indicate that any server that implements the right end-points is a PDS. (For example, the Blacksky team's rsky project, written in Rust, includes rsky-pds.).

Self-hosting a PDS means you have to index the entire network.

It has been revealed that A PDS only stores its own accounts' data. Indexing the network is the job of relays and AppViews — a self-hosted PDS uses someone else's. (In Bluesky's PDS software, PDS_CRAWLERS defaults to https://bsky.network, and PDS_BSKY_APP_VIEW_URL defaults to https://api.bsky.app.).

According to recent reports, that is why the hardware is small. The official PDS instructions recommend 1 GB of memory, 1 CPU core, and a 20 GB SSD — for 1 to 20 users. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Every record on the network is a Bluesky post.

A repository can hold records of any type — any lexicon, from any app — all mixed together in the same user's repository. Calendar events, bookmarks, blog posts, game state, workout logs, or a custom app's own schema: each is just another collection. (And, by default, a PDS accepts records whose lexicon it does not know — “optimistic validation”.).

For example, my repository (reiver.blacksky.team) has these collections, according to com.atproto.repo.describeRepo:.

Only one of those 14 collections is Bluesky posts (app.bsky.feed.post). Even among Bluesky's own record types, most are not posts — likes, reposts, follows, lists, a profile. And, actor.rpg.* and equipment.rpg.item are from a different app altogether. (See: ATProto Record.).

Recent findings suggest that the author is the repository the record is in. (See: ATProto Record.).

A record key is unique within a repository.

“The tuple of (did, rkey) is not unique; the tuple (did, collection, rkey) is unique.”.

A tid record key tells you when the record was created.

“Record keys are "user-controlled data" and may be arbitrarily selected by hostile accounts.” Do not trust them as timestamps.

A record's createdAt is when it was created.

Industry observers note that it is whatever the client put there. The app.bsky.feed.post lexicon describes it as a “Client-declared timestamp”.

Records can contain floating-point numbers.

Floats are not allowed in the data model — they do not round-trip reliably, and the bytes must be exact for hashing.

You can compute a record's CID by hashing its JSON.

Recent findings suggest that the CID is a hash of its DRISL-CBOR encoding. JSON is not byte-exact.

A missing field and a null field mean the same thing.

They are different — and both are different from false, 0, or an empty array.

Every record in a repository is valid against its lexicon.

By default, a PDS only checks records whose lexicon it knows (“optimistic validation”, or “fail-open”). Validate what you read.

A record with fields its lexicon does not mention is invalid.

Unexpected fields should be ignored — “at worst as warnings”. (Validating a post with an extra mood field against app.bsky.feed.post passes. See: ATProto Lexicon.).

A deleted record leaves a tombstone.

“Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or "tombstone" of previous contents.”.

An NSID is an address you can fetch.

It is a name — a reversed Internet domain plus a name. (See: ATProto NSID.).

It is safe to lowercase an NSID.

Industry observers note that the Internet domain part is not case-sensitive, but the name is — getRecord is not getrecord. “Implementations should not force-lowercase NSIDs.”.

Implementations reject an NSID whose Internet domain part is longer than 253 characters.

The specification claims 253 — but the official test vectors list a 283-character one as valid, and Bluesky's TypeScript and Go code only check the 317-character total.

If _lexicon.feed.bsky.app does not exist, try _lexicon.bsky.app.

Lexicon resolution is not hierarchical. If the exact record does not exist, resolution simply fails. (See: How-To Resolve a Lexicon.).

The app.bsky.* lexicons are in the bluesky-social/atproto repository on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that not anymore — its main branch has no lexicons/app/bsky/ directory. Resolve them from the network instead (they are published by did:plc:4v4y5r3lwsbtmsxhile2ljac).

A union in a lexicon lists every type you will ever see there.

In a recent development, unions are open by default — new types can be added. (The live app.bsky.feed.post lexicon's embed union includes app.bsky.embed.gallery, which older code will not know about.).

It can change — in compatible ways (new optional fields, more union types, etc).

You need a special library to talk ATProto.

In a recent development, XRPC is plain HTTP and JSON. curl works. (See: ATProto XRPC.).

A server returns the error names listed in the end-point's lexicon.

Not always. resolveHandle's lexicon lists HandleNotFound, but public.api.bsky.app answered an unknown handle with InvalidRequest.

The specification itself warns that “many services will return generic load-balancer or reverse-proxy HTML error pages.”.

An end-point a server does not have returns 404.

A Bluesky PDS answered a made-up end-point with 401 AuthMissing.

A cursor means something you can use.

Industry observers note that treat it as opaque. (One server's listRecords cursor happens to be the last record key — do not depend on that.).

In a recent development, every PDS has its own firehose, and there are several relays — for example, Bluesky's bsky.network and the Blacksky team's atproto.africa. (See: ATProto Relay.).

A user's PDS knows who follows them.

Recent findings suggest that A follow is an app.bsky.graph.follow record — stored in the follower's repository, with the followed account's DID as its subject. So, a user's PDS knows exactly who the user follows, but not who follows them — those records are spread across everyone else's repositories, on every PDS. (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

It is one service's opinion. For the same account (reiver.blacksky.team), at the same time (November 22nd, 2026), public.api.bsky.app (Bluesky's AppView) said 292 followers, api.blacksky.community (the Blacksky team's AppView) said 196, and the Constellation backlink index said 134. (See: ATProto AppView and How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

With enough work, a follower count can be computed exactly.

You would have to check every repository on every PDS — and you can never be sure you found them all, since a relay only knows the hosts it crawls. By the time you finished, the answer would have changed. And, what counts as a follower is a choice — for example, the app.bsky.graph.follow lexicon notes “Duplicate follows will be ignored by the AppView.” (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

A feed generator sends you posts.

It sends a skeleton — a list of post URIs. The AppView fills in the posts. (See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

A label is a signed annotation. What to do with it (hide, blur, warn, nothing) is up to each app and user. (See: ATProto Labeler.).

Account status (active, deactivated, etc) can be verified cryptographically.

“Unlike other aspects of atproto, account status is not self-certifying”. It is passed along hop by hop — so different services may disagree. When in doubt, ask the account's own PDS (com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus).

Bluesky is one app built on it. Others use their own lexicons — for example, site.standard.document, community.lexicon.location, and actor.rpg.sprite.

ATProto is a microblogging protocol.

According to recent reports, microblogging (short posts, like Bluesky's) is just one thing built on it. The overview describes ATProto as “a decentralized protocol for large-scale social web applications”. Nothing in the core protocol is about posts — records, repositories, XRPC, and sync work the same for any record type. What a record is comes from its lexicon, and anyone with a domain can define new ones.

For example: long-form documents (site.standard.document), locations (community.lexicon.location), game sprites (actor.rpg.sprite), custom feeds (app.bsky.feed.generator), and, in the spaces proposal, bookmarks, private forums, and group chats. Even the protocol's own lexicons are published as records (com.atproto.lexicon.schema).

(Falsehoods that come from comparing ATProto with ActivityPub, the Fediverse, and Mastodon.).

Unlike ActivityPub (and the Fediverse, and Mastodon), ATProto does not use JSON-LD.

DID documents are JSON-LD. plc.directory serves them with the content type application/did+ld+json, and each one starts with an @context:.

According to recent reports, (That is from plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz. A did:web document has one too — for example, api.bsky.app/.well-known/did.json.).

Recent findings suggest that what is true is that ATProto's own data — records, lexicons, XRPC — is not JSON-LD. And, ATProto software usually reads DID documents as plain JSON — the ATProto DID specification indicates which fields to read, and does not call for JSON-LD processing.

Like on Mastodon, an ATProto handle includes the user's server — @user@server.

On Mastodon, a user's full address is a user name and a server — Mastodon's documentation says it is “in the form @username@domain”, and that “@user@example.com is not the same as @user@example.org.”.

According to recent reports, an ATProto handle is just one domain name — like reiver.blacksky.team — and it says nothing about the user's server. The server (PDS) is found separately, from the DID document. (A handle shown as @reiver.blacksky.team has just one @, as a decoration.).

ATProto has nothing like a Fediverse “instance”.

According to recent reports, the difference is that it is more hidden. It is not part of the user's identity or handle — reiver.blacksky.team does not say which PDS hosts it. It is not what decides what a user sees — that is mostly the AppView. And, a user can move to another PDS while keeping the same DID, handle, posts, and followers.

Like Mastodon, ATProto looks up handles with WebFinger.

Mastodon uses WebFinger (/.well-known/webfinger) — its documentation states “WebFinger is required for fully interoperating with Mastodon.”.

Sources indicate that ATProto does not. A handle is resolved with a DNS TXT record at _atproto., or with https:///.well-known/atproto-did. (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Like on Mastodon, when a user moves to a latest server, their posts stay behind, and their followers have to be moved over.

On Mastodon, moving an account moves followers — but Mastodon's documentation says “Your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations”, and that “Mastodon presently does not support importing posts or media”. Moving also has to “force everyone to unfollow your current account and follow your new account”.

In a recent development, on ATProto, moving to a new PDS includes “migrating data from the old PDS to the new PDS” (from the accounts specification) — the whole repository, posts and all. And, the account keeps the same DID. Since follow records point at the DID, followers do not have to be moved at all. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Like ActivityPub servers, ATProto servers send posts to each other's inboxes.

In ActivityPub, a server pushes each activity to its recipients — the ActivityPub specification describes it being “inserted into the actor's inbox (delivery)”, by HTTP POST.

Like in ActivityPub, to trust a copy of a post, you have to check it against the server it came from.

The ActivityPub specification claims servers should do “something at least as robust as checking that the object appears as received at its origin”, and that “No particular mechanism for verification is authoritatively specified”. (Mastodon uses HTTP Signatures, to check who sent an activity.).

Industry observers note that ATProto data checks itself. Repository commits are signed with the account's key, and records are identified by their hash (CID) — so a copy can be checked no matter who it came from. The data model specification says this “makes it possible to redistribute content and trust copies even if coming from an untrusted party.” (See: ATProto Record.).

ATProto and the Fediverse cannot talk to each other.

In a recent development, they are different protocols — but there are bridges. For example, Bridgy Fed describes itself as “a decentralized social network bridge. It connects the fediverse, the web, and the Atmosphere (Bluesky).” With it, people on one network can follow, reply to, like, and repost people on the other.

(These are about the spaces proposal, which is not yet part of the specification.).

Today, yes — but the spaces proposal adds data that only some people may read.

In a recent development, “Atproto spaces provide access control, not confidentiality. They are not end-to-end encrypted.”.

A space is stored on one server.

Each member's records stay on that member's own PDS. “The space does not colocate records on a single network host.”.

A copy of space data proves who wrote it.

Space data is authenticated with MACs, not signatures — on purpose, so that it “should not carry proof of authorship that survives a leak outside its access boundary.”.

Most of these come from the same idea: ATProto separates things that are usually tied together.

So, the safe defaults are: key everything by DID; resolve, do not assume; validate what you read; ignore what you do not understand; and expect other servers to disagree with yours.

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • According to recent reports, in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

According to recent reports, in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Recent findings suggest that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's fresh speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It has been revealed that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

Recent findings suggest that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Industry observers note that parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

It has been revealed that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

In a recent development, to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

In a recent development, each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Sources indicate that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Recent findings suggest that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who noted what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

Industry observers note that we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's fresh is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Recent findings suggest that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

In a recent development, urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

According to recent reports, the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

It has been revealed that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

According to recent reports, you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

According to recent reports, raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Sources indicate that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Sources indicate that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

According to recent reports, like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Problems and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

AI Governance in 2027: Accountability Moves Into the Workflow

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them.
  • It has been revealed that that gap will become harder to defend in 2027.
  • According to recent reports, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them. They ask for a review. Somewhere inside the organization, a policy names an accountable executive—but the support team cannot find anyone authorized to change the result. Governance exists on paper. The person is still stuck.

It has been revealed that that gap will become harder to defend in 2027. As AI moves into ordinary operations, accountability will have to become something an organization can exercise while a disputed decision is still affecting someone's life.

According to recent reports, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations. My expectation for 2027 is that buyers will ask for evidence of these practices inside operating workflows. The following predictions concern organizational accountability, rather than a promise that a particular checklist can make every AI system fair.

The most revealing name on an AI governance chart is the person who can say stop. In 2027, more organizations will describe roles with genuine authority to suspend or change a deployment. That changes the meaning of ownership: responsibility becomes a decision right, with consequences for a project somebody else may be eager to keep running.

Industry observers note that responsibility without authority creates a ceremonial owner. A governance lead can maintain an inventory while a product team changes the model, a supplier changes the service, and an operations team changes the decision threshold. No single person necessarily controls the consequences of the resulting system.

The Govern function in the NIST framework connects roles and organizational risk management. The NIST Playbook offers practical actions that organizations can adapt. These are voluntary resources, not evidence that adopters already execute them well.

According to recent reports, the development I expect is a more concrete chain of authority: who can accept a use case, who can narrow its scope, and who can stop it when the evidence changes. Different decisions can belong to different roles. What matters is that the authority survives ordinary commercial pressure and is exercised against a documented standard. A well-written responsibility chart that nobody uses would not demonstrate the predicted change.

According to recent reports, look for published suspension criteria, records of actual governance decisions, and escalation paths beyond the product's revenue owner. A policy naming an accountable executive without explaining what that executive can change would provide weaker evidence than an operational case study.

Assign decision rights before expanding a deployment. Buyers should ask who can authorize exceptions and whether the risk function can halt a workflow without the supplier's consent. Founders can shorten enterprise reviews by making these responsibilities visible in the product and service agreement.

Sources indicate that an explanation can tell someone why a decision happened and still leave them powerless to correct it. I expect enterprise products to make challenges more practical in 2027, preserving the original evidence and recording what the reviewer decides. The test of the feature will be what happens after the person notes the system has missed something notable.

It has been revealed that an explanation and an appeal solve different problems. An explanation tells a person what supposedly happened. An appeal gives them a route to change an outcome that may be wrong, incomplete or inappropriate for their circumstances. A generic support form can satisfy neither need if the reviewer cannot reconstruct the original decision.

The OECD guidance treats due diligence as a continuing process involving impacts and responses. That makes remediation a useful commercial design question as well as an ethical one. My forecast is that some vendors will turn it into a repeatable workflow rather than leave each customer to improvise.

Sources indicate that the difficult part will be the reviewer's independence and access to context. Re-running the same model with slightly different wording is not a meaningful challenge process. Nor should preserving evidence require indiscriminate retention of sensitive personal information. The system needs enough decision context to support correction while honoring appropriate retention and access limits.

Recent findings suggest that look for the ability to submit missing facts, reach a qualified human reviewer, and receive a recorded disposition. Reversal rates and time to correction will be more revealing than the existence of an appeal button. Unanswered queues would weaken the forecast's practical significance.

It has been revealed that budget for the people who handle contested decisions. A supplier's automation savings should be assessed alongside review workload and correction costs. Product teams should design evidence capture and access permissions with the appeal process, because reconstructing decisions afterward can be expensive or impossible.

An internal drafting assistant can become a customer-screening tool through a series of apparently small product decisions. The launch approval may still be on file while the use case has changed underneath it. In 2027, more governance programs will revisit material changes in models, data and affected populations, treating approval as a continuing responsibility.

A system approved for drafting internal correspondence can become consequential when its output starts determining which customers receive an offer. The model may be unchanged; its social role has changed. Conversely, a supplier revision can alter behavior while the customer-facing workflow looks identical.

In a recent development, ISO/IEC 42001 addresses organizational AI management, and ISO's discussion of 42001 and impact assessment connects management practices with evaluating effects. Neither makes a management-system certificate a guarantee that every output is accurate or every deployment is acceptable.

According to recent reports, the practical challenge is proportionality. Repeating a full assessment for a spelling correction would overwhelm the process; ignoring a upcoming affected population would undermine it. Organizations will need a defensible account of which changes alter the risk and which do not.

Look for specific reassessment triggers and examples where a deployment's conditions were narrowed after review. Version logs alone will be insufficient. Evidence that organizations compare real effects before and after a material change would strengthen this prediction considerably.

In a recent development, include change notification and evaluation rights in supplier contracts. Internally, connect the model inventory to the systems that manage deployment changes. The objective is to identify changes that matter early enough to act, without turning every routine maintenance event into a board-level decision.

A certificate can become more reassuring than the evidence warrants. The harder commercial conversation is what it actually covers. In 2027, assurance and procurement documents will become clearer about the difference between an organization's management practices and the behavior of a particular deployment. That precision will make assurance more useful, even when it makes the sales claim less sweeping.

The more popular a governance label becomes, the more tempting it is to treat that label as a universal seal of safety. Yet different assurance exercises answer different questions. An audit of management processes cannot prove that a model behaves reliably for a population the evaluator never tested.

ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems. It is relevant to the quality of certification itself. It does not turn ISO/IEC 42001 into a product-performance benchmark. This distinction will become more commercially important as suppliers use assurance credentials in sales processes.

My confidence is lower here because incentives can favor broad reassurance over careful qualification. Still, sophisticated buyers have a reason to demand both organizational assurance and use-case evidence: they bear the consequences if a certified supplier's product fails in their workflow. Good assurance should make the remaining questions clearer, rather than imply that there are none.

Look for an explicit statement of the certified entity, scope, exclusions and validity period, alongside separate application testing. Claims that a certificate proves an AI system is unbiased or universally compliant would run against the direction predicted here.

Recent findings suggest that use certification to inform diligence, then evaluate the actual deployment. Suppliers should prepare a clear explanation of what their assurance covers. Buyers should ask which unresolved risks remain their responsibility and what evidence would justify accepting them.

Sources indicate that accountability becomes visible when the organization has a reason to resist it: an attractive launch, an expensive correction, a profitable use case that needs narrowing. The strongest governance stories in 2027 will show how those decisions were made—and whether the people affected had a meaningful way to be heard.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • Industry observers note that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

Industry observers note that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That mentioned, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

According to recent reports, for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Recent findings suggest that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing revealed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Navigation, parking, driver monitoring and speed handling also change in this release.

Parking location selection can draw on personalized parking history, and the map can display multiple parking options at the destination.

Tesla also lists improved detection of road signs, small animals, road debris and chains, along with potholes, road details and avoidance of deep standing water. Speed handling changes cover each driver profile, school zones, speed limits and inclement weather, and FSD can slow for speed cameras.

Recent findings suggest that for driver monitoring, Tesla reports greater availability of vision-based attention monitoring when drivers wear hats or sunglasses, with reduced strictness in higher-speed driver profiles. Autoshift now uses FSD-based gear predictions, and Bike Rack Mode allows drivers to enable FSD with bike racks or similar hitch accessories.

FSD v15 couples a new control interface with changes to the vision and driving systems. The planned wider release will test whether Tesla’s reported intervention improvement is sustained as those changes reach more drivers.

Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets Through Its "Don't Ask Again" Feature

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets Through Its "Don't Ask Again" Feature.
  • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.
  • Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets Through Its "Don't Ask Again" Feature.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The tech giant identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.

The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file .claude/settings.local.json, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.

It has been revealed that when [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.

On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.

The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.

The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.

Industry observers note that apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".

Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone noted AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".

User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:.

Recent findings suggest that while this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.

Recent findings suggest that at very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json and adding it to the repo's .gitignore, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • In a recent development, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

In a recent development, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to proposal for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Recent findings suggest that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

Industry observers note that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

Sources indicate that the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. Fresh public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an vital part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Recent findings suggest that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

Recent findings suggest that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

In a recent development, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

Sources indicate that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

According to recent reports, we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

One person familiar with the matter interpreted the team cap as an attempt to prevent leaks and stated banks found ways to work around it.

In a recent development, spaceX’s June 2026 IPO provides the closest comparison in the report. Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two banks that led both IPOs, declined to comment. SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Why is email marketing important?Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.2. What is benefits of email marketing?Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:Better brand recognitionStatistics of what works bestMore salesTargeted audienceMore traffic to your products/services/newsletterBuild credibilityMost  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide. 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.5. How do I write a decent subject line?The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free. 6. Is email marketing still effective?Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience. 7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them. 8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your customers' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.10. Where can I find email template?Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use. However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.Final Saying You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

The robot completes the pick. The audience applauds.
